title: Catfish Stew, Nupe Style
author: Ronke Adeyemi
desc: Catfish arranged in a single layer, seasoning sprinkled over rather than stirred in, covered with warm water and cooked twenty minutes to a thick smooth stew.
longDesc: This is the one Nupe-attributed recipe in the collection, written by an author who identifies herself as Nupe and explains why catfish is central to the cooking of Niger, Kogi and Kwara states — rivers and swampy ground. The method respects the fish: it is cut into five or six pieces, slimed with hot water, patted dry, and then arranged in a single layer over fried onions with the stock cube and dried pepper sprinkled over the top rather than mixed in. Warm water to cover, twenty minutes, and the cue is a thicker smooth stew.
steps: Chop the catfish into five to six pieces.
Pour hot water over the pieces to remove the slime, then rinse in cold water and pat dry.
Heat the oil in a saucepan and fry the onions for one minute.
Arrange the fish in a single layer over the onions.
Sprinkle the bouillon cube and the dried pepper over the fish.
Pour in warm water to cover and cook on medium heat approximately 20 minutes, until you notice a thicker smooth stew.
Add salt to taste and serve.
chefTips: Hot water over the fish first for the slime, then cold to rinse, then pat dry. Catfish slime will make the whole stew cloudy and slightly muddy.
A single layer, and leave it alone. Catfish falls apart the moment you start moving it.
Sprinkle the seasoning over the top rather than stirring it in. It dissolves down through the liquid without you having to disturb the fish.
Warm water, not cold. Cold water into a hot pan with fish in it will seize the flesh.
A thicker smooth stew is the cue, at about twenty minutes. The fish releases gelatine and the liquid tightens on its own.
Only one minute on the onions. This is a quick dish and the onions are there for aroma, not for a browned base.
Four tablespoons of palm oil for one fish is generous and correct — it is what makes the stew read as a Nigerian stew rather than a poach.
commonMistakes: Stacking the fish or stirring it.
Mixing the seasoning in and breaking up the fish.
sources: Adapted from 'Catfish Stew – Nupe Style!', byline Ronke Edoho, 9jafoodie. Quantities exactly as printed: 1 catfish; 1 medium onion (finely chopped); 1 tablespoon dried chilli powder; 1 Knorr cube; 4 tablespoons of palm oil; salt to taste. Yield not specified.

Method as printed: chop the catfish into five to six pieces; pour hot water over the pieces to remove slime, rinse in cold water and pat dry; heat oil in a saucepan and fry the onions for one minute; arrange the fish in a single layer; sprinkle the Knorr cube and dried pepper over the fish; pour warm water to cover and cook on medium heat approximately 20 minutes. DONENESS CUE as printed: 'until you notice a thicker smooth stew'. Serving as printed: 'Serve with rice or Tuwo Shinkafa'.

THE PROVENANCE IS THE VALUABLE PART: the author identifies herself as 'a Nupe girl and proud', notes that the Nupe inhabit Niger, Kogi and Kwara States, and explains that catfish is 'very common in Nupe dishes' because of the region's rivers and swampy areas. For a region where almost nothing is documented, a named Nupe author writing about her own tradition is a significant find.
FLAGGED: no Nupe-language name is given for the dish. It is titled in English and attributed to Nupe style, which is weaker than a local name.

THE NUPE RECORD IS OTHERWISE EMPTY. Searches for EMIGBIRI returned ZERO results — no recipe, no description, no mention. Searches for KUCHELA likewise returned NOTHING. Those two dishes were specifically sought and the record is blank; they are not published here.
This author is therefore the best Nupe lead available, and her site's other recipes may contain further Nupe material that is not labelled as such in search results.
healthBenefits: Catfish is a lean source of protein and omega-3 fats.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
No thickener or flour of any kind.
culturalNote: The Nupe live along the Niger in Niger, Kogi and Kwara states, and their cooking reflects it — catfish is an everyday ingredient rather than a special one. That this is the only documented Nupe recipe reachable anywhere, written by an author claiming the tradition as her own, says more about the state of the written record than about the cuisine.
